HOMAGE TO SHAHEED-E-WATAN, ASHFAQULLAH KHAN 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon'ble Members, today is the Martyrdom Day of 
Shaheed-e-Watan, Ashfaqullah Khan, a great martyr of "Kokori Rail Dacoity 
Case." Ashfaqullah Khan belonged to the stream of nationalism which 
glorified India's stuggle for freedom with the blood of martyrs. He was the 
forerunner, who inspired Bhagat Singh and others in their revolutionary 
activities. Ashfaqullah Khan participated in the Kakori Rail Dacoity, 
alongwith Pandit Rama Prasad Bismil and eight others. He also participated 
in the raids by the revolutionaries at Sherganj, Bichpuri and Mainpuri, and at 
other places. 
Ashfaqullah Khan, alongwith Rama Prasad, Roshan Singh and Rajendra 
Lahiri, was sentenced to death in the Kakori Rail Dacoity case. The Kakori 
case trial brought the entire nation together to defend Ashfaqullah and his 
revolutionary comanions. The British Government did not yield to any 
appeals made by the leaders. Ashfaqullah, Rama Prasad Bismil and Roshan 
Singh were executed on the 19th December, 1927. All three greeted death 
bravely with a smile. 
This year also happens to be the birth centenary of Ashfaqullah Khan, and 
in this year and on this martyrdom day, it is important for all of us to recall 
and revive our glorious struggle for freedom. Nation owes a debt of gratitude 
to these revolutionaries for their sacrifice. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence in memory of 
Shaheed-e-Watan, Ashfaqullah Khan. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute}

Development of Air-Strip Near Dehradun 
† *421. SHRI MANOHAR KANT DHYANI: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is no developed and improved airstrip in 
Uttaranchal, a newly created State; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that an air-strip at Jolly Grant near Dehradun, 
the capital of the State, which is being used at present, is suitable for small 
aircrafts like Dornier only; 
(b) whether Govenrment would upgrade this air-strip to make it 
suitable for operation of normal aircrafts keeping in view the 
significance of formation of a new State; and 
(d) if so, by when and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) 
to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
STATEMENT 
(a) and (b) Airports Authority of India (AAI) has got two airports in the 
State of Uttaranchal, one at Jolly Grant near Dehradun and another at Pant 
Nagar which are fully operational and suitable for operation of Dornier 228 
type of aircraft. Dehradun and Pant Nagar airports are not suitable for 
operation of bigger aircraft. 
(c) and (d) The State Government of Uttar Pradesh had been 
asked as early as in 1992 to confirm whether it can transfer 112.35 
acres of land free of cost for further development of Jolly Grant 
airport to make it suitable for operation of B-737 class of aircraft. Till 
date the land has not been made available to the Airports Authority 
of India. Details of the proposal have now been taken up with the 
Government of Uttaranchal.

*422. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the 11th Finance Commission recommended 
the winding-up of the National Fund for Natural Calamity and setting-up of 
a National Calamity Contingency- Fund; 
8 

[19 December, 2000]       RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have accepted this recommendation and if so, 
when; 
(d) when and in what manner this will be implemented; and 
(c) how the contingency of natural calamity of rare severity will be 
addressed pending the creation of NCCF? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (e) A statement is laid on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. The Central Government's role is to supplement the efforts of 
the State Governments for calamity relief. In its recommendations 
concerning calamity relief, the Eleventh Finance Commission has increased 
the size of the Calamity Relief Fund (CRF) to Rs. 11007.59 crores, 
compared to Rs. 6304.27 crores under the Tenth Finance Commission, with 
contributions from Centre and States in the ratio of 75:25. EFC has invisaged 
that with the increased transfers under the CRF. States should be able to 
provide immediate relief to the victims of cyclone, drought, floods, 
hailstorm, earthquake and fire. The new NCCF scheme has been provided 
for only calamities of rare nature and extraordinary severe intensity. 
(b) The EFC has recommended creation of National Calamity 
Contingency Fund (NCCF) in the Public Account of the Government of 
India with an initial corpus of Rs. 500 crores as contribution from the 
Government of India. Drawals from the Fund arc to be recouped by the 
imposition of a special surcharge. Assistance from the Fund is to be 
provided for calamity of such a severe nature that would call for financial 
assistance to the affected State over and above what is available in the CRF 
or other Plan/ Non-Plan sources. 
(c) The report of the EFC was laid on the Table of the House on 27th 
July, 2000. The recommendations of Eleventh Finance Commission have 
been accepted by the Government. 
(d) and (e) Guidelines for the ad ministration of the National 
Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF) have been issued. The Scheme

of Finance has moved for the raising of Rs. 500 crores through a

Session of the Parliament. The Scheme also envisages setting up of National 
Centre for Calamity Management under the Ministry of Agriculture to 
monitor extent of natural calamity and recommend releases of assistance to 
States from the NCCF.

*423. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of guidelines worked out for implementing the Kelkar 
Committee recommendations on complete deregulation of the oil sector by 
2002, privatisation of all oil and gas P.S.Us. by 2005 and norms of subsidy 
suggested on L.P.G. and Kerosene to be 15 per cent and 20 per cent, 
respectively, of import parity; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the present subsidy on L.P.G. and Kerosene 
works out to be 25 per cent and 45 per cent of import parity, which is much 
higher than the Kelkar Committee's recommendation; and 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
19 

RAJYA SABHA        [19 December, 2000]  
Statement 
(a) The Government in January 1995, had set up the Kelkar 
Committee to make recommendations on strategic restructuring plan 
of the oil sector. The Committee had inter-alia recommended phased 
reduction in subsidies on domestic LPG and kerosene for public 
distribution and total deregulation of the downstream petroleum 
sector by 31st March, 2002. However, it did not make 
recommendations on norms of subsidy on domestic LPG and 
kerosene for public distribution. Similarly, it did not recommend 
privatisation of all oil and gas PSUs by 2005. 
However, an Expert Technical Group (ETG) was set up by the 
Government in June 1996. The ETG inter-alia recommended a year-by-year 
programme for reduction in subsidies on domestic LPG and kerosene for 
public distribution. After considering the recommendations of ETG, 
Government in November 1997 decided that subsidy level on domestic LPG 
will be reduced to 15% of import parity by 2000-2001; and on kerosene for 
public distribution to 33.33% of the import parity by 2001-2002. On full 
deregulation i.e. effective 1st April 2002, the subsidy on domestic LPG and 
kerosene for public distribution will be transferred to fiscal budget of the 
Government. 
(b) The estimated average subsidy for December 2000, based on 
November 2000 international prices of crude oil and products, is 48% on 
domestic LPG and 53% on kerosene for public distribution. 
(c) Subsidies vary with the changes in the international oil arid product 
prices. Due to high volatility in the international prices of crude oil and 
petroleum products since February 1999, the subsidy level has increased 
inspite of upward revisions in the consumer prices of domestic LPG and 
kerosene for public distribution.

Measures to prevent dumping of palmolein 
*425. SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken any steps to increase the basic import 
duty on crude Palm Oil; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what are the steps taken by Government to avoid the dumping of 
palmolein in Indian Market? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. The import duty 
(inclusive of surcharge) on crude palm oil imported for the manufacture of 
vanaspati was 16.5% since December, 1999. On 
26 

[19 December, 2000]       RAJYA SABHA 
21st November, 2000, this duty was increased to 25%. The import duty 
(inclusive of surcharge) on crude palm oil imported for any other use, which 
was 50.8% since June, 2000, was also increased to 55% on the same day. 
These changes were carried out through notification nos. 142 to 144/2000-
Customs all dated 21st November, 2000 which have already been laid on the 
Table of both Houses on the same day. 
(c) Under the customs law dumping is said to occur when any goods are 
exported at a price below the price at which they are sold in the domestic 
market of the exporting country. Anti-dumping duty is imposed, in such 
cases, if it is found on investigation that goods have been dumped causing 
injury to the domestic industry. No such complaint of dumping has been 
received by the Government in respect of palmolein.

indications of some slowdown in selected sectors of industry in recent months 
for various reasons, including the sharp increase in international oil prices 
and relatively weak monsoon. As per the Index of Industrial Production (IIP) 
the overall industrial growth during April-October 2000 has been 5.7% 
(aided by 5.8% growth in manufacturi ng, 4.6% in electricity and 7.5% in 
mining) compared to 6.7% in April-October 1999. As per use-based 
classification, consumer durables and basic goods performed better whereas 
capital goods and intermediate goods performed less welt. 
The Government has undertaken a series of measures to boost investment 
confidence. These include mobilization of over US$ 5.5 billion through 
Indian Millennium Deposits (IMD), rapid reforms in key sectors such as 
telecom and textiles and sound fiscal management.

Bank's earlier commitments to provide employment to applicants particularly 
orphans or whom bank did riot offer any financial help to sustain; 
(b) if so, why these applicants were not exempted from failing under the 
purview of revised rule and what is bank's vested interest to decline such less 
number of cases; and

those children who fulfil Bank's criteria applicable prior to 20th March, 1997 
to help such needy persons? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) Punjab National Bank have 
intimated that they have revised their scheme for compassionate appointment 
keeping in view the observations of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in its 
judgement dated 4.5.1994. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in its judgement has 
observed that "the compassionate appointment cannot be granted after a lapse 
of reasonable period which must be specified in the rules. The consideration 
for such employment is not a vested right' which can be exercised at any time 
in future. The object being to enable the family to get over the financial crisis 
which it faces at the time of the death of the sole bread winner, the 
compassionate employment cannot be claimed and offered whatever the lapse 
of time and after the crisis is over". 
Accordingly, bank had made a provision in their revised scheme that the 
cases of the dependants of the deceased employees can be considered at the 
discretion of the bank within 4 years of the death of the employee. The 
revised scheme has been made applicable w.e.f. 20.3.1997 and all pending 
applications have been examined keeping in view the provisions of the new

revival and development of the traditional sources of water such as Aahar,

(c) No, Sir.

Water Resources and submitted a memorandum urging them for

[19 December, 2000]        RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) Non-plan Assistance of Rs. 2.50 crore was released to M/s 
National Projects Construction Corporation Ltd. (NPCC Ltd.) before Durga

Identification of rivers causing floods 
† 3298. SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH: 
 SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have identified those rivers which cause heavy 
losses almost every year due to floods in the country; 
(b) if so, the names of such rivers; 
(c) the annual quantum of flow of water in these rivers; and 
(d) the quantum of water for the utilisation of which projects have been 
constructed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) 
Rashtriya Barh Ayog constituted by Government of India, in its report 
(1980) has identified the following rivers which are prone to floods. 
1. Brahmaputra Region; The Brahmaputra, the Barak, the Teesta, the 
Torsa & the Jaldhaka. 
2. Ganga Region; The Ganga, the Sharda, the Ghaghra, the Gandak, the 
Burhi Gandak, the Bagmati, the Kamla, the rivers of Adhwara 
Group, the Kosi, the Bhagirathi, the Ajoy and the Damodar. 
3. Central India and Deccam Region; The Brahmani, the Baitarni, the 
Subaranarekha, the Tapti and the Narmada.Coastal areas (deltaic 
Regions) of Mahanadi and Godavari rivers also experience flood. 
(c) and (d) As per assessment made by the Central Water Commission, the 
average annual flow available in these river basins is about 1389.4 Billion 
cubic Metre (BCM) out of which 474.4 BCM is utilizable. The total live 
storage capacity of dams and reservoirs completed on these rivers is about 
86.5 BCM.

government out of their own resources and as per their priorities.

SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Mr. Chairman, 
Sir, I am grateful to the Prime Minister and the hon. Members who 
have participated in the discussion on the Motion moved by me. When 
I was listening to the Prime Minister, I expected that some of the issues 
which have been raised by me and my colleagues would be responded 
to by him in the proper perspective. Mr. Chairman, Sir, the Prime 
Minister talked of numbers, and indicated why we have brought this 
Motion under Rule 170, because the number is in our favour. Sir, most 
respectfully, I would like to submit for the consideration of the Prime 
Minister that in Parliamentary democracy, number is important. He has 
more than 272 in Lok Sabha, that is why he is the Prime Minister. We 
don't have 272 plus, that is why we are in the Opposition. This is the 
ground reality. Mr. Prime Minister, you are Prime Minister because of 
the number. You accepted this Motion under the corresponding rule 
184 in the other House because you had the number. Therefore, 
please don't try to belittle the number. It has its relevance in 
Parliamentary democracy. You have raised this question. A number of 
participants from the ruling side asked why we are repeatedly raising 
Ayodhya. We are raising it not to disrupt the nation, not to divide the 
communities, but to ensure that the provocative utterances which are 
coming from your allies, from your leaders, the sinister activities, which 
are going on for the construction of the temple at the disputed site, 
sending alarm signals, which we don't want. We are apprehensive of it. 
You are a cultured man, a scholarly man. Even as a student of class X, 
you wrote a beautiful poem. But Mr. Prime Minister, a Prime Minister 
can be a poet, but he must be a statesman; and we require - ■ 
statesman. We expected that, in you, we will find a statesman who will 
steer out in a vexed situation. Who is doubting your own belief? 
Nobody. From day one, from 1992 onwards, you are entitled to 
consider that your colleagues are innocent. You have advised us, and 
very correctly advised us, that propriety should not be confined only to 
Delhi; it should move from Delhi to Bihar. May I most respectfully 
submit 
228 

[ 19 December, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
to the Prime Minister, through you, Mr. Chairman, Sir, in 1998, when 
you formed the Government, you appointed some persons who were 
chargesheeted, who stood chargesheeted, at that point of time. 
Nobody raised this question because it is exclusively your prerogative. 
Surely, as Members of this House, we cannot dictate to you to take 
A.B.C or D in your Council of Ministers. You are the sole arbiter; you 
are the sole master. You appointed some persons who stood 
chargesheeted, but what happened later? After some time, two of 
them were dropped. Surely, I would not like to mention their names; 
everybody present in this House knows their names. Two of them 
were dropped; till today, they have not been found guilty by the court. 
The court had not pronounced any judgment against them, at least, at 
the point of time when you dropped them, but you dropped two of them 
and retained some. There comes the question of propriety which is 
being used selectively. That is the question. If it was not selective, if it 
had been applied uniformally, if the same yardstick had been applied, 
if two were dropped, others were not retained, the question would not 
have come. 
What is the contention in the motion? Have you found even a 
single word, where we have recommended, saying that you accept the 
resignations of the three members of the Council of Ministers? 
Perhaps, you are mixing the Motions of this House and that of the 
other House. In this House, the Motion has totally and completely 
concentrated on your observations only. I do agree, Sushmaji also 
pointed out. My problem, as a listener is the way she delivers her 
speech, her command over the language, and, above all, her 
charming personality simply sweeps me off. But, after listening to her, 
when I analyse it in my mind, I find it extremely difficult to get at the 
points. Yes; the Prime Minister is fully entitled to have a belief, as an 
individual. But the limited question which we raised and debated was, 
as a Prime Minister, can you afford to say something which sends a 
wrong signal and which creates confusion? Yes; the presspersons will 
ask you question; they will grill you. But, as a custodian of so much 
information - you know a lot of it; you are the best judge; you are not 
new to the job; you are a veteran politician; you are one of the oldest 
politicians of the country and you have an illustrious record at your 
credit-is it appropriate that when some press people ask some 
questions, you find it obligatory on your part to reply to it and to 
respond to it in a way that creates confusion? if you read any 
newspaper, Mr. Prime Minister--this is not an impression which we 
alone are carrying; almost each and every newspaper  is  carrying  the  
same  impression--several  clarifications  were

diffusing the tension in Jammu and Kashmir and that talks would 
begin. We have welcomed it. We have welcomed it and we wish you 
all success there, it is not correct to say that there is lack of

THE CENTRAL ROAD FUND BILL, 2000 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF ROAD 
T R A N S P O R T    A N D    H I G H W A Y S    ( M A J .    G E N .    ( R E T D . )    B . C .    
KHANDURI): Madam, I move : 
'That the Bill to give statutory status to the existing Central 
Road Fund governed by the Resolution of Parliament 
passed in 1988, for development and maintenance of 
national highways and improvement of safety at railway 
crossings, and for these purposes to levy and collect by 
way of cess, a duty of excise and duty of customs on 
motor spirit commonly known as petrol, high speed diesel 
oil and other matters connected therewith, as passed by the 
Lok Sabha, be taken Into consideration." 
Before 1 make a request to pass the* Bill, with your 
permission, 1 would Hke to say a few words. Madam, in our country, 
there Is a vast network of roads, stre tching to over 3.3 million km, that 
Is, about 33 iakh km of roads. Out of this, there are 57, 737 Kms of 
National Highways. The development of roads In this big country has 
not realty kept pace, the way, it should have, basically because of 
paucity of funds. And therefore, a long term strategy, a sustained 
Ananda! arrangement.had to be made, and for development of roads, 
this sort of exercise had to be carried out. I may put across to the non. 
Members that such a concept did exist for a long time. The Central 
Road Fund first came 4nto existence in 1920, and thereafter, it 
continued. Some money was collected which was very meagre even 
for roads. But it was in 1077 that the Parliament passed a Resolution 
and decided that not less than 3.5 paisa per litre of petrol should be 
levied for the purposes of development of roads In this country. This 
went on, and at this rate, we collected about Rs. 25 to 30 crores per 
year, which was being distributed in the ratio of 80:20 to the States 
and the Centre. Subsequently, In May 1988, another Resolution was 
passed by the Parliament, according to which not less than 5 per cent 
of the cost of petrol and diesel was to be levied for the purposes of this 
Fund. This cess was to be distributed In the ratio of 64 per cent to the 
States, 35.5 per cent to the Centre and half a per cent for the 
administration of this Fund. However, this Resolution was never 
implemented from 1988 toi998. This remained unimplemented 
because it was all the time under examination, and for some reason or 
the other,  it could  not  be Implemented.     Thereafter, in  1998,  a 
cess was 
247 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2000] 
introduced for petrol at the rate of one rupee per litre. This was during the financial 
year 1008-99, and it was effective from 2nd June, 1998. In the subsequent year, 
1999-2000, a cess on diesel was also introduced at the same scale, that Is, one 
rupee per litre, and it became effective from 1st March, 1999. The allocation norms 
for this Fund were also decided, and according to them, out of the diesel 
collection, 50 per cent, that is, 50 paisa would go straight to the rural roads 
through the States. The balance 50 per cent, plus the cess on petrol would again be 
combined, and of this, 57.5 per cent would be given to the Centre, 30 per cent to 
the States, 12-1/2 per cent to the Railways for the purposes of providing safety at the 
level crossings, constructing railway over-bridges etc., and thus, it was distributed to 
the States as well as to the Centre. Out of the 30 per cent to be given to the 
States, 3 per cent was kept aside by the Centre for the purposes of developing 
within the States inter-State roads or places of economic importance, and thus, 
this cess was introduced and the distribution was made. Now, a question has 
come up here, and there was also an observation about the Ordinance. I would 
tike to explain this thing to the House. Although I agree in principle that an Ordinance 
should not be Issued when the Parliament is about to meet, but in this case, I 
would like to Inform the House that it was done in good faith and with good 
intention. The reason was that this money was available but we had no legal 
instrument to distribute it In the way I have just mentioned. Therefore, this decision 
was taken. This money was available. The States were saying that soon after the 
monsoon, they will be demanding the money. The working season was available 
after October- November, and therefore, if we had to wait, in that event, we would 
have lost two months, the month of November and December, because it was 
required to be passed here, then the normal procedure was to be followed, and 
probably, by January, we would have been able to allot the money. I would like 
to inform the House that because of the Ordinance, Rs. 990 crores have been 
sub-allotted to the States, out of which, one-third has already been distributed. 
Therefore, the aim of this Ordinance was that we make money available to the 
States. Many State Chief Ministers have written letters requesting that money be 
made available. .There was a working season, and that is why, the first Instalment 
has been sent, and therefore, I inform the House that this Ordinance has been 
issued with good Intention. The salient features of this Bill are four. Firstly, it gives 
statutory status to the Central Road Fund and to the Resolution of 1988. Secondly, 
this Fund will go straight to the Consolidated Fund, and thereafter, the 
Parliament will enable It to be

distributed In the ratio which  I  have Just  now  mentioned.  Thirdly,  
the distribution of the cess has been now fixed in the Bill, and it 
cannot be denied, ft cannot be used or misused for any other purpose. 
Finally, this Fund is non-lapsable. With these words, Madam, I request 
that the Bill be taken into consideration. Thank you.

the present Minister for having brought this Bill. The only thing is that it

necessary for the development of the entire nation, in accordance with 
the other development activities that many Central Governments have

SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL: Madam, the Chit Funds Act, 
1982 was enacted as a Central Act for ensuring uniformity In the 
provisions applicable to the Chit institutions throughout the country, 
providing for certain built-in operational safeguards for Chit operation 
and for protecting the interest of Chit subscribers. Chit Fund is basically 
an arrangement to promote savings and their utilisation for mutual 
benefit of the members of the Chit. The State Government, in 
consultation with the Reserve Bank of India, makes rules under the Act, 
which is administered by the officials and authorities of the State 
Governments concerned. The Act has so far been extended to 16 
States and six Union Territories.

The Constitutional validity of the Act and its various provisions 
were challenged in various courts. The Supreme Court in its judgment 
dated 13th July, 1993 upheld the constitutional validity of the Act and 
inter-alia commented that the 'appropriate authorities, in case the 
demand is so raised from time to time, increase the limits of aggregate 
amounts of chits under section 13 of the Act. Keeping in view the 
comments and suggestions received from some of the State 
Governments, the All-India Association of Chit Funds and the 
observations of the Supreme Court, the following amendments to the 
Chit Funds Act, 1982 are being proposed. 
Sub-section 3 of Section 6 of the Act prescribes for maximum 
amount of discount not to exceed 30 per cent of the chit amount which 
the prized subscriber has to forego. It is proposed to enhance the 
ceiling of discount from the existing 30 per cent to 40 per cent. 
Section 13 of the Act prescribes limits of aggregate chit 
amount for different types of foremen. Keeping in view the observation 
of the Supreme Court, it is proposed to increase the limit of aggregate 
chit amount for individual foreman fr om Rs.25,000/- to Rs. 1,00,000/- 
and in the case of partnership and association of individuals, from Rs. 
1,00,000/- to Rs.1,00,000/- per partner, subject to a ceiling of 
Rs,6,00,000/-. 
Section 20 of the Act provides for every foreman to deposit an 
amount equal to the chit amount in the name of the Registrar in an 
approved bank for obtaining permission and operating and conducting 
the chit. It is proposed that the amount which the foremen has to 
deposit with the Registrar can be deposited to the extent of 50% in 
cash and balance 50% in the form of bank guarantee. With these 
words, I commend the Bill for consideration of the House. 
Madam, this is a simple Bill. Therefore, I don't think there is 
any need to send it to a Select Committee or to the Standing 
Committee. As it is pending for a long time, I request the House that it 
may be taken into consideration and passed unanimously.

clauses which are proposed to be amended. 
Madam, the value of the rupee has gone down to less than 
four paise in the last two decades. It is getting reduced day by day. So, 
it is necessary to accommodate for the devaluation of the rupee. I feel 
that the revision of the aggregate amount of the chit seems 
reasonable. The chit fund is a sa fer and simple system of savings and 
credit. A subscriber joining a chit, while he is subscribing, is promising 
that a certain amount of money will be deposited as security, till the 
maturity of the chit. While subscribing to the chit, he creates a right to 
get the aggregate amount during the course of the chit. Perhaps, if he 
is lucky, he can get the amount at the very beginning itself. He is not to 
pay any interest on it, because the system is like that. If a subscriber 
to a chit is in need of money, he can auction the chit. The limit for the 
auction is demarcated by the percentage of discount. The discount, 
according to the mother Act, is 30%. We all know fat the rate of 
interest in banks is coming down. Then, what is the purpose of 
increasing the discount from 30% to 40%? The cost of money ^ would 
become more. It is not good to increase the discount percentage. 
We know that to get a loan from a nationalised bank is very 
difficult for a common man. Even though the Government controls the 
majority shares in the nationalised banks, it is very difficult. When the 
banks are privatised or when the Government shareholding is made 
less, then it will be much more difficult for the common people to get 
any loan from a commercial bank. 
The cooperative sector is not widespread enough to cater to 
the credit needs of the common man. So, the system of chit fund 
should be encouraged. There are so many chit fund organisations in 
the country, and not all of them are registered with the Registrar, as 
envisaged in the Act. There are so many chit fund companies and they 
are mushrooming. They are opening their offices in far off places like 
Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, parts of Delhi, parts of U.P., to get rid of 
the restrictions that are imposed by the Bill. 
282 

[ 19 December, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
I demand that the Government should come forward with a 
proper regularised operation of the chit funds so that the subscriber

enhancing the discount from 30 to 40 per cent. I request the 
Government to withdraw this clause. The last point that 1 would like to 
mention is that the security amount with an approved bank is 100 per

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI) : 
Madam, I move: 
"That the Bill to consolidate and amend the law relating to 
juveniles in conflict with law an d children in need of care and 
protection by providing for proper care, protection and 
treatment by catering to their development needs, and by 
adopting a child-friendly approach 
292

in the adjudication and disposition of matters in the best 
interest of children and for thei r ultimate rehabilitation through 
various institutions established under this enactment, as 
passed by Lok Sabha,   be taken into consideration," 
Madam, the Juvenile Justice Act, 1986 enacted by Parliament 
to provide for care, protection, development and rehabilitation of 
neglected or delinquent juveniles has been in force since 2nd October, 
1887. The Government felt that provisions of the Act were not 
addressing the issues of care and protection of neglected children 
adequately. 
The revision of the current Act has been pending for sometime 
and a review of the Act and its implementation over the years revealed 
a number of deficiencies/shortcomings warranting extensive 
amendments in the Act. The Bill which is now before this august 
House for consideration is an attempt to make the judicial system 
more child friendly and accessible to a juvenile/child or anyone on 
their behalf, including the police, voluntary organisations, social 
workers or parents and guardians throughout the country,  and provide 
for rehabilitation of the destitute child. 
The present Juvenile Justice Act, 1986 Is not in conformity 
with International Conventions on the Rights of the Child, ratified by 
India, such as the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, the 
United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Administration of 
Juvenile Justice, 1995. These Conventions have prescribed a set of 
standards to be adhered to by all State parties in securing the best 
interests of the child. CRC being a subsequent development to the

the Act. Therefore, it was decided to bring forth a fresh Bill    before 
this august House replacing the present   Juvenile Justice Act, 1986. 
I would like to highlight the salient features of the proposed 
Bill which are as follows: - 
(1) It would separate the Act into two parts - one for juveniles in 
conflict with law; and the other for the juvenile/children in 
need of care and protection which will give the clarity and 
distinction in the treatment. 
(2) The    proposed    Bill    will    make    the    justice    system    
for juvenile/children more appreciative of the developmental 
needs in comparison to criminal justice system as applicable 
to adults. At the moment, we treat all children, those who 
are abandoned and destitutes,  as potential criminals. 
(3) It brings the juvenile law in conformity with the CRC. It 
prescribes a uniform age of eighteen years for both boys 
and girls,   as per article 1 of CRC 
It ensures speedy disposal of cases within a limited period of 
four months. It spells out the role of the State as a facilitator rather 
than a doer by involving voluntary organisations and local bodies in 
the implementation of this Act. It proposes creating special juvenile 
police units. This is for the first time that we have suggested this in 
India that we have child-friendly police units, with a humane approach 
through sensitisation and training. It would enable increased 
accessibility to juveniles by establishing the Juvenile Justice Board 
and the Child Welfare Committees and Homes in each district or 
group of districts. It contains effective provisions for various 
alternatives for rehabilitation and so cial reintegration, such as 
adoption, foster care, sponsorship and aftercare of abandoned, 
destitute, neglected and delinquent juveniles, as provided in articles 
18 to 21 of the CRC. I hope that with the enactment of the Bill, the 
children in need of care and protection, would get a better deal. At 
least, they will get coverage by law which they do not have, at the 
moment. With the creation of ad equate infrastructure for the 
implementation of the Act, with the involvement of informal systems, 
especially the family, voluntary organisations and the community, our 
objective to treat the children in the best possible manner
